messages.subject: Specifying parameters for DIF anaylsis
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm running a series of DIF analyses using a graded response model for a 21-item measure with a 7-point Likert scale and ran into a problem. I tested all the items in calibration sample and cross-validation sample, coming away with 17 items and parameters for the focal sample. I fixed the parameters for the focal sample and began testing for DIF in the first comparison sample using the drop method. However, when I got to the step of constraining the slopes and intercepts and freeing the hyperparameters, the model was not identified and the DIF analysis would not run. I am guessing that having no items freely estimated in the focal sample is producing the error? Is there a way to test DIF when the parameters are fixed in the focal sample?

Thanks,
Daniel

messages.subject_clean: Scoring the general factor in a bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I am interested in scoring the general trait of the bifactor model in the simplest possible way (preferably so that it can be used by clinicians with limited statistical knowledge). I recently read the paper 'DeMars 2013: A Tutorial on Interpreting Bifactor Model Scores' and my interpretation is that once controlling for the specific factors, the coefficients from the general factor can be used independently to create the score. This confuses me since the bifactor model is compensatory in nature.

What is your opinion?

Best,
Rico

"In some contexts, the bifactor model may be chosen because the user wants to
interpret the general trait scores, controlling for nuisance factors. For example,
on an attitude survey, the negatively worded items might load on a specific factor,
as in Kim and colleagues’ (2011) study of a Korean adaptation of measures of
adult attachment. For this type of use, trait score estimates on the general factor
will represent more pure measures of the trait of interest after controlling for
this negative-wording factor." DeMars 2013

messages.subject: Re: Itemfit - Empirical plots - itemGAM
messages.body_plain:
There's isn't always a way to save poorly fitting items. The functional forms could be quite complex, non-monotonic, contain step functions, and so on. So sometimes, we just have to admit that some items do not fit well, and ask whether their inclusion is still justifiable even with some misfit. That said, I don't see a huge problem with this item in terms of the point-wise diagnostics. As well, so long as the RMSEA for the SX2 statistic is reasonably low relative to the other items then you may be justified in keeping it in your test. Probably not the most exacting advice you wanted to hear :)

Phil

Regrading deciding whether a DIF item is significant or not, I wonder how should we decide between sDRF and uDRF? If neither of them is significant, do we say the DIF is not significant? Yingyi

messages.subject: Re: a few questions around DRF
messages.body_plain:
I assume you mean sDTF and uDTF (I didn't create any statistics called sDRF and uDRF). And no, these aren't quite the same thing. My original development of those DTF statistics were limited in that they were required to have an arbitrary bounded range of integration (otherwise, in some cases they could become degenerate), and didn't include whom was being affected by the bias (information that comes out of the density function for theta). This is why the later developments in the DRF() function should be seen as much better, as they are more in line with magnitudes of effect size rather than the area-based measures. HTH.

Phil

So, I'm interested in using mIRT in a very practical sense.  I've got a background in educational research and I'm fine with unidimensional IRT, but I mostly do 2pl models in STATA.  Totally unfamiliar with R, downloaded it and RStudio, got the mIRT package installed, and an hour of frustration and red errors later, threw up my hands and admitted my ignorance. I'm not a measurement expert nor am I going to publish in this area, and I'm mostly interpreting results for an audience with very little measurement experience.

What I want to be able to do is run bifactor models on live test data.  For example, I have a test from a biology professor with n=207 students, 30 items, and a belief that 7 of those items load on two constructs (critical thinking and biology knowledge) while the other 23 items just have the single factor (biology knowledge).  I'd like to be able to produce this sort of graph (found on the web) for those 7 items.  Ideally, theta-hats for both biology knowledge [from all 30 items] and critical thinking [from the 7 flagged items] would also be nice.

I think what I'm looking for is a "getting started" guide.  I found the wiki and was not having much luck replicating the code in there, but it is VERY possible that I'm doing things wrong.  Does anybody have a suggestion for a new person on where to start, if getting to this sort of model is the end goal?

For the redirect portion, I think just defining the final_page input to include a hyperlink to the website you are trying to direct traffic to would be sufficient.

Ideally I do not want to expose the server.R function to front end users because this interface must be highly controlled for CAT sessions to work properly (as opposed to more general shiny applications). I suppose some question are in order to determine how to control this behaviour:

1) Would this GET request be initialized at runtime, or must this be updated throughout the CAT session?
2) Could this GET call be avoided if in the initial script the fetching occurred and were simply passed to mirtCAT as user-define custom variable to be accessed when needed?
3) What is the end goal here, how do you plan on using this ID variable index in your application?

messages.subject: Re: Scoring the general factor in a bifactor model
messages.subject_clean: Scoring the general factor in a bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
DeMars' interpretation is correct, and yes you should be able to use the scores from a bifactor model's general factor independently. The idea is that the specific factors act as a type of residual covariance, and after accounting for these redundancies any left over common variation must have been due to the general factor. Computing the factor scores also accounts for this residual dependency effect so long as the specific factors are jointly included during estimation. So, while you're correct that the traits are compensatory, so long as the factor score components are modeled jointly then the inflation that would have occurred without these specific factors (e.g., fitting a unidimensional model) will provide more 'purified' estimates of the dominant trait. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Specifying parameters for DIF anaylsis
messages.body_plain:
The limitation of the DIF() search, especially in the more exploratory scheme you're in, is that it is possible for the scheme to become non-identified without providing anchor items. The next release of mirt actually will throw a warning if it suspects the search will be tending to this problem (among other new features for this function). Your best solution might be to start in the opposite direction via the 'add' schemes, and work your way up from there. It's less efficient in terms of parameter estimates (not necessarily a problem if your sample size is large enough), but shouldn't have this problem occur. HTH.

Phil
